text.text: An employee is frequently absent, late, or leaving early in a pattern affecting their work and team. Straightforward when policy is clear — complex when protected leave is involved.

• An employee who has called out 8 times in 10 weeks with no medical documentation.
• Someone consistently 30–45 minutes late despite two prior verbal conversations.
• Absences that cluster around Mondays and Fridays in a recurring pattern.
• An employee who leaves early several times a week without prior approval.
• A team member whose unplanned absences are causing coverage gaps for the rest of the team.
• Someone who has exhausted their PTO balance and continues calling out.
• An employee who calls out frequently but refuses to provide any explanation.
• A remote employee who is repeatedly unavailable during core hours without notice.
Gather and preserve these records as you work through the check.

1. Keep a running attendance log with exact dates, times, and any reason given by the employee.
2. Note when you notified the employee and what their response was — in writing, even a quick email.
3. Save any documentation the employee provided (doctor's notes, text messages, emails).
4. Record whether each absence was excused or unexcused per your policy.
5. If a pattern is emerging (e.g. always Mondays), note the pattern explicitly in your log.

elements.text: You can attach files and links securely from the completed assessment before submitting it to HR.

text.text: Watch for: Absences that may qualify as FMLA, ADA accommodations, or state-protected leave. Disciplining an employee for protected absences is one of the most common HR legal mistakes.
Contact HR: If the employee has mentioned a health condition, family care responsibility, or anything that sounds like it could be protected — contact HR before issuing any discipline.
